newsitem.title: USA: U.S. expects Kabila cooperation in U.N. probe.
newsitem.headline: U.S. expects Kabila cooperation in U.N. probe.

text.p: The United States on Thursday refused to accept reports that Congo President Laurent Kabila has told some local officials to do as little as possible to aid a U.N. investigation into alleged refugee massacres by his troops.

"What we know is quite a bit different and that is that in talks with (U.S.) Ambassador (Bill) Richardson and separately in talks with U.N. Secretary General Koffi Annan, Mr. Kabila agreed to U.N investigations of reported massacres of refugees," spokesman John Dinger told reporters.
"And we expect him to keep his word and we fully expect him to cooperate fully with U.N. investigations," he said.
Dinger added: "I don't think we have any reason frankly to expect that" Kabila will not keep his pledge.

The spokesman was responding to a report in the Washington Post that Kabila, new president of the country formerly known as Zaire, has told some local officials to do as little as possible to aid a U.N. inivestigation into alleged refugee massacres by his troops.

Citing unnamed Western and Congolese sources, the Post said Kabila and other representatives of his Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo gave the warning at an unusual meeting in the town of Bukavu last weekend.

They told government officials from Kivu Province, on Congo's eastern border with Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi, "not to direct human rights investigators to any mass grave sites or potential witnesses," the Post said.

It cited its sources as saying Kabila and his new government were under intense pressure from Rwandan and Ugandan security officials to stymie the probe. Rwandan and Ugandan security forces formed an important part of Kabila's armed uprising against President Mobutu Sese Seko, who fled into exile on May 16.

In exchange for help in toppling Mobutu, Kabila was forced to give those units a free hand in gunning down thousands of ethnic Hutu refugees, who had been living in what was then Zaire since 1994, the sources were quoted as saying.

Dinger said Assistant Secretary of State John Shattuck, who oversees human rights issues, met in Rwanda on June 10 with Rwandan Vice President Paul Kagame "who promised full Rwandan cooperation with the U.N. investigation."

He noted that during an earlier attempt by a U.N. commission to enter eastern Congo "Rwanda did cooperate on that occasion (and) so we have a pledge from Rwanda as well as a record of Rwandan cooperation."

As for Uganda, Dinger said U.S. officials have been in touch with the government there and expect it to also cooperate with the United Nations but he did not know if an official committment had been provided.
